title: Habits live in places
hook: habits are tied to contexts, which is why holidays break routines (Wood and Neal)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the loop of cue, routine, reward, and the click at the start where a habit is easiest to see.

A vacation. A rented room by the sea, a different bed, a different kitchen, no commute. Somewhere in there, the morning run that never gets skipped at home quietly stops happening. So does the evening stretch, and the glass of water before bed. Nobody decided to quit. Then the suitcase comes home, the key turns in the old lock, and some of those habits switch back on almost by themselves. It works the other way too: a habit someone has fought for years can loosen on a trip. Today's idea explains both.
screen: `A DIFFERENT BED, A DIFFERENT KITCHEN.` → `THE MORNING RUN STOPS.` → `THE KEY TURNS, IT COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: First, the place is part of the habit. Psychologists Wendy Wood and David Neal argue that habits are tied to their contexts: the room, the time, the people around, the thing just done. The context works like yesterday's cue. Walk into the kitchen, and the kitchen starts the routine. Second, change the place and the habit can slip. Wood and her colleagues followed students who moved to a new university. Where the new setting looked like the old one, habits like exercising or watching television tended to carry on. Where it changed, habits were more likely to break, and intentions mattered more. A holiday is that same experiment, run on yourself. Third, it cuts both ways. A move, a new job, even rearranged furniture can be the moment a stuck habit lets go, because the old cues are gone, or the moment a good one gets lost. Fourth, a set-aside place. In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus tells his listeners, in the King James words: "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret." His point is praying in secret rather than for show, not habit. But the picture is a set-aside place: a closet, a shut door. A cushion in one corner, a chair by one window, can work on the principle the researchers describe. Practice something often enough in one spot, and the spot itself starts helping.
screen: `THE PLACE IS PART OF THE HABIT.` · `A NEW CAMPUS, OLD HABITS SLIP.` · `IT CUTS BOTH WAYS.` · then, large: `ENTER INTO THY CLOSET.`

segments.voice: Look around: is this a spot you could come back to tomorrow, and the day after, a particular chair, a corner of the bed, a step on the back porch? If it is, sit here on purpose and feel the light, the sounds, what's under you; if it isn't, picture the place that could be and sit with that picture. Either way, rest on the breath and let the place soak in.
Habits live in places. A habit is tied to its setting, so a new place can break it, and a chosen place can hold it. Today's word.
Your line: the place holds it. A trip can loosen a habit, and a chosen corner can keep one. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: Some people who keep a daily practice set aside one place for it, a corner, a chair, a cushion, a prayer space, and return there each day, so the setting itself becomes part of the habit.

notes: Confirm the description of Wood, Tam and Witt: students transferring universities; habits (exercising, reading the paper, watching TV) persisted when the new context was similar and were more likely to be disrupted, with intentions guiding behavior more, when it differed.
